sources.title: Anishinabek Nation, Who Are the Anishinaabeg?
sources.note: Community education page, headings Big Ideas, The Anishinaabeg territory, Nswi-Shkodewin, and Political Territorial Organizations: diversity, shared territories, regional names, Ojibwe as one Anishinaabe group, and modern organizations.

sources.title: National Park Service, History & Culture: Grand Portage National Monument
sources.note: Sections Gichi Onigaming and Homeland of the Grand Portage Anishinaabe: ancient route, Grand Portage Band identity, Ojibwe and Anishinaabe naming, land knowledge, technology, incursion, divided jurisdictions, and continuity.

sources.title: Mark David Spence, Native Ground, Middle Ground, Battle Ground: The River Raisin, the War of 1812, and the Course of North American History
sources.note: National Park Service historic resource study, chapter 2, printed pages 33 to 65: sixteenth-century regional networks and disease, seventeenth-century displacement, Great Lakes communities, diplomacy, and evidence limits.

sources.title: The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents, volume 23
sources.note: Colonial missionary transcription, Relation of 1642 to 1643, printed pages 223 to 225: Pauoitigoueieuhak invitation, 1641 journey, Sault population, Algonquin language, neighboring peoples, farming, and missionary purpose.

sources.title: Wisconsin Historical Society, Timeline of Wisconsin history, 1622-1699
sources.note: Institutional timeline, entries 1659 to 1661: Radisson and Groseilliers at Chequamegon Bay and Mille Lacs, Ojibwe wintering reference, Huron displacement, and Menard mission chronology.

sources.title: Michael Witgen, Place and Belonging in Native North America
sources.note: An Infinity of Nations, chapter 1, pages 29 to 68, especially opening 1660 gathering at Odaawaa Zaaga’igan and analysis of place, belonging, Anishinaabeg communities, and political geography.

sources.title: Michael Witgen, The Rituals of Possession and the Problems of Nation
sources.note: An Infinity of Nations, chapter 2, pages 69 to 108, especially the June 14, 1671 French ceremony at the Anishinaabe Sault village, fourteen attending nations, and conflict between colonial possession and Native political realities.

sources.title: Michael Witgen, The Rebirth of Native Power and Identity
sources.note: An Infinity of Nations, chapter 3, pages 116 to 167: later-seventeenth-century Anishinaabe-Dakota relations, La Pointe communities, trade, mobility, alliance, conflict, and Native political action.

sources.title: Michael Witgen, The Great Peace and Unraveling Alliances
sources.note: An Infinity of Nations, chapter 6, pages 267 to 314, especially the 1701 gathering at Michilimackinac, approximately two hundred canoes, Montreal journey, diplomacy, and aftermath.

sources.title: National Park Service, Archeology: Grand Portage National Monument
sources.note: Sections The Meadow and Archeological Investigations: at least two millennia of occupation evidence, archaeological work, changing uses, preservation, and limits of assigning deposits to a single modern identity.

sources.title: Cecile R. Ganteaume, Infinity of Nations: Art and History in the Collections of the National Museum of the American Indian
sources.note: American Indian Art Magazine, autumn 2010, printed pages 60 to 62: regions are not bounded or static; late-seventeenth-century French phrase infinity of nations; Anishinaabe seasonal movement, plurality, exchange, and sovereignty.

sources.title: Anishinabek Nation, About Us
sources.note: Community organization page, Anishinabek Nation and History sections: present organization scope, Three Fires history, distinct Ojibway, Odawa, and Potawatomi roles, Great Lakes relations during the 1600s and 1700s, and later institutional change.

sources.title: National Park Service, Historic
sources.note: Institutional overview, early French contact section: Brule around 1622, Nicolet in 1634, Raymbault and Jogues in 1641, sparse immediate effects, and cautions about the timing of Great Lakes change.

sources.title: National Park Service, Home of the Ojibwe
sources.note: Apostle Islands page, Home of the Ojibwe section: Madeline Island, seasonal fishing, hunting, wild rice, maple sugar, spring plants, selected medicinal plants, and living regional identity.

sources.title: Great Lakes Indian Fish & Wildlife Commission, Ojibwe Treaty Rights: Understanding & Impact
sources.note: Fifth edition, foreword and printed pages 7 to 12: eleven-band scope, seasonal camps, food gathering, extended families, winter teaching, sharing, clan responsibilities, and explicit modern treaty-rights purpose.

sources.title: 1854 Treaty Authority, Wild Rice
sources.note: Official intertribal authority page, opening and Wild Rice Survey, Monitoring, Traditional Harvesting and Finishing, and Resource Guide sections: manoomin significance, ecosystem knowledge, protection, restoration, cooperation, harvesting resources, and present management scope.

sources.title: The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents, volume 54
sources.note: Colonial missionary transcription, Relation of 1670 to 1671, printed pages 127 to 133: Sault fishery, Pahouitingwach Irini, Outchibous, multiple nations, seasonal gathering, hunting, and the source’s evangelizing purpose.

sources.title: National Park Service, Harvestable Species Plan: Apostle Islands National Lakeshore
sources.note: Final environmental assessment, printed pages 31 to 35: consultation, Ojibwe movement between islands and mainland, hunting and plant knowledge, regional band participation, and modern management context.

sources.title: National Park Service, Minnesota: Grand Portage National Monument
sources.note: Sections on Grand Portage Ojibwe seasonal preparation, birchbark winter and warm-season lodges, extended families, canoes, fishing, hunting, and adoption of Native travel technology; interpretive reconstruction rather than a household census.

sources.title: National Museum of the American Indian, Canoe model, catalog 5/1145
sources.note: Catalog record NMAI_55228: Anishinaabe Chippewa/Ojibwa attribution, circa 1900 inferred Great Lakes provenance, birchbark, wood, conifer-root materials, folded, carved, and stitched techniques, dimensions, and uncertain collection history.

sources.title: Canadian Museum of History, The Birchbark Canoe (1603)
sources.note: Virtual Museum of New France page: Champlain’s 1603 description, light birchbark construction, shallow-water travel, French adoption of Indigenous transportation, and a seventeenth-century image identified separately from later objects.

sources.title: Bruce M. White, Grand Portage as a Trading Post: Patterns of Trade at the Great Carrying Place
sources.note: National Park Service commissioned 2005 report, preserved by Park Archives. Trade Patterns and The Invention of the Great Lakes Fur Trade, printed pages 6 to 13: traditional and French accounts, goods, and uncertain first Ojibwe-French encounter.

sources.title: Frances Densmore, Chippewa Customs
sources.note: Bureau of American Ethnology Bulletin 86, based mainly on 1907 to 1925 work. Printed pages 22 to 29 dwellings; 44 to 48 treatment and health measures; 48 to 52 infant care. Later ethnography is never silently back-projected.

sources.title: National Museum of the American Indian, Smithsonian in Your Classroom: Native Dolls
sources.note: Fall 2004 education issue, printed pages 11 to 15: dolls and learning, object interpretation, Ojibwe doll materials, birchbark uses, cradleboards, and the modern educational frame.

sources.title: Anishinabek Nation, Classroom Activity 2
sources.note: Community education page, Anishinaabe Chi-Naaknigewin and Dodemaag System sections: One Anishinaabe Family, named clan roles, governance teaching, Elders Council authorship, and modern instructional setting.

sources.title: Anishinabek Nation, About Early Learning Child Care
sources.note: Current community program page: 39 First Nations, child and family support, land-based learning, language revitalization, educator development, locally varied programming, and First Nations control.

sources.title: Ojibwe People’s Dictionary, nibi
sources.note: University of Minnesota dictionary search result, entry nibi, part of speech ni, translation water, speaker and regional variation notice, and project credits. Used as a modern Latin-orthography sample only.

sources.title: National Park Service, Ojibwe Ethnobotany
sources.note: Voyageurs National Park page: by the early 1700s Ojibwe people in the park area used plants for food, medicine, ceremonies, and materials; the page explicitly warns that practices vary by place, time, participant, and recorder.

sources.title: Anishinabek Nation, Health Secretariat Programs and Services
sources.note: Current community program page, IHWS Programs, Healthy Babies Healthy Children, Community Wellness Workers, and Healing Lodges sections: First Nation autonomy, family and maternal support, referrals, traditional and contemporary approaches, and modern dates.

sources.title: National Park Service, Mni Owe Sni (Coldwater Spring)
sources.note: Current official place page, Introduction, History, and Additional Information sections: living cultural-place status, spring and riverbank, Dakota, Anishinaabe, Iowa, and Ho-Chunk gathering, present tribal partnerships, and current nonpotable-water warning.

sources.title: Great Lakes Indian Fish & Wildlife Commission, Indigenous Knowledge
sources.note: Community institution page, opening and Anishinaabe Insights sections: localized knowledge of ecology, animals, plants, seasons, harvesting, stories, songs, place names, policy work, and limits on generalizing distinct knowledge systems.

sources.title: Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, The Ojibwe Learning Center and Library
sources.note: Official tribal page, Kinoomaage Miinwaa Gindaaso Gamig section: current books, cultural objects, birchbark canoes, language classes, events, and community space, last updated February 21, 2024.

sources.title: Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe, Culture
sources.note: Official Band page, History and Culture section: current language and culture schooling, Elders in classrooms, assisted living, craft teaching, wigwam building, sugarbushing, hunting, fishing, ceremonies, and explicit continuity.

sources.title: Anishinabek Nation, Our Story, Our History
sources.note: Community page, paragraphs on residential, day, and industrial schools, forced child removal, language suppression, survival, remembrance, and present transmission. Used for later colonial disruption and living continuity, not early-modern description.

sources.title: The Jesuit Relations and Allied Documents, volume 52
sources.note: Colonial missionary transcription, Relation of 1668 to 1669, printed pages 199 to 205: Sault and Pointe du Saint-Esprit missions, trade travel, displaced nations, councils, women and children, and strongly judgmental evangelizing language.

sources.title: Government of Canada, The Arrival of the Europeans: 17th Century Wars
sources.note: Official military-history chapter, Great Lakes conflict and Great Peace sections: colonial alliances, Indigenous raids and losses, 1697 context, August 4, 1701 treaty, negotiated compromise, and limits of surrender narratives.

proposedOverrides.name: “Obiwa” atlas layer (probable Ojibwe association)
proposedOverrides.summary: Approximate 1530 to 1715 atlas layer labeled “Obiwa,” cautiously associated with Ojibwe history but not treated as a surveyed border, centralized state, or complete Anishinaabe homeland.
